paras: The lynching of Clyde Ellison was the hanging of a Black man by a mob from a bridge about three miles from Star City, Arkansas, on a Friday morning in mid-June 1919. A Star City report blamed an alleged attempt to attack a young woman, but a Century News Service dispatch said Ellison was killed for refusing to work for a white farmer for 85 cents a day and that the assault charge was a plot. Black papers reported that he was tortured with heated flat irons and left hanging overnight under a warning sign, and the Colorado Statesman named the killing in an editorial on recent outrages.

According to the Century News Service dispatch, dated June 20 at Star City, Ellison lived in the neighborhood and had been offered 85 cents a day to work in a cotton field for a white farmer. When he refused, it was thought that he could be frightened into accepting the work, and a charge of assault on Idelle Bennett, the 18-year-old daughter of Dave Bennett, was placed against him. The dispatch said the girl "gave the plot away" when she admitted that her father had told her of Ellison's refusal and of the part she was to play in the scheme to force him to pick cotton.

After what the dispatch called a final appeal to Ellison, he was seized, carried to a bridge, and a rope was tied around his neck. Flat irons were heated and placed on his naked body, and he was forced to jump off the bridge; the fall broke his neck. His body was left hanging overnight with a sign tacked to his head, and the sheriff and deputies were then notified to come and cut it down. The Star City report printed in the Cleveland Advocate placed the hanging on Friday morning at a point about three miles from town.

The Star City report said that none of the members of the mob had been identified. The Century News Service dispatch said instead that everyone who took part was known locally, since the town was so small that people could be recognized by their voices. It added that all of Bennett's farm labor had left him and that the farms in the surrounding country were deserted. No report of an inquest, arrest or trial appears in the coverage.

The killing reached the Black press through two separate reports, both printed on June 21. The Cleveland Advocate ran a brief Star City item dated June 18 that gave the accusation of an "alleged attempt" to attack a young woman, and its editor appended the remark that this was "the usual 'cock and bull' story that accompanies a jynching notice." The Chicago Defender carried the Century News Service dispatch on its front page with the subhead "Lynchers Give Warning," presenting the assault charge as a scheme to force Ellison into the cotton fields.

The Colorado Statesman took up the case in a June 28 editorial, "The Darkest Hour," which listed the "cold-blooded, barbarous, savage-like actions" of the Star City mob, Ellison put to death for refusing to work for 85 cents a day, among recent attacks on Black people in the South. On July 5 the Statesman reprinted the full Century dispatch on its front page, beside an account of the beating of a Black army lieutenant in Little Rock. The two printings of the dispatch differ on the sign: the Defender's text reads "This is how we treat you," while the Statesman's reads "This is how we treat lazy niggers."

The accounts disagreed on why Ellison was killed: the Star City report gave an alleged attempt to attack a young woman near her home, while the Century dispatch said the assault charge was invented to frighten him into field work and that the young woman admitted the scheme. They also differed on the lynchers, whom the Star City report called unidentified and the Century dispatch said were known to everyone in town.

accounts.label: Star City report (June 18)
accounts.gist: Ellison was hanged to a bridge Friday morning three miles from town after an alleged attempt to attack a young woman near her home; no mob members were identified. The Cleveland Advocate's editor added that this was the usual 'cock and bull' story.

accounts.label: Century News Service dispatch (June 20)
accounts.gist: Ellison was lynched for refusing to work for a white farmer for 85 cents a day; the assault charge on the farmer's daughter was a scheme she admitted; he was tortured with heated flat irons, hanged from a bridge, and left with a sign; all participants were known locally.

framing.detail: The Cleveland Advocate printed the Star City accusation but its editor dismissed it as 'the usual "cock and bull" story that accompanies a jynching notice.'
The Chicago Defender ran the Century News Service dispatch on page one under 'Lynchers Give Warning', presenting the assault charge as a plot to force Ellison to pick cotton.
The Colorado Statesman called the Star City mob's acts 'cold-blooded, barbarous, savage-like' in its editorial 'The Darkest Hour' and later reprinted the full dispatch.
